notes.body:
The questioner has identified a genuine puzzle. The epistles (رسائل) of the Brethren of Purity (إخوان الصفا) state that a solar eclipse happens only at the **end of the lunar month** — the moon must reach conjunction with the sun near the month's close before a new crescent can rise. Yet eclipses were also observed at the first days of Ramadan, which seemed to violate this rule entirely.

The Imam called "the author of the letters" is the same Imam — or the Imam under whose authority — those epistles (رسائل) were produced. In Ismaili understanding, these letters were composed within and guided by the mission (دعوة), so the Imam and the letters form **a single source of knowledge**, encountered at different moments rather than two competing voices.

Appealing to the Imam therefore resolves rather than restates the problem. A written text is sealed at the moment of its writing. The Imam's living word can do something no fixed text can: **expand and complete it**. The epistles (رسائل) gave one half of the astronomical picture — the end of the month. The Imam's transmitted clarification adds the other half: a solar eclipse may also fall at the beginning of the month. This is not a contradiction of the letters; it is the fuller truth the letters had left unspoken.

There is a quiet astronomical point beneath this too. In a visibility-based lunar calendar, "the end" of one month and "the beginning" of the next describe the **same astronomical moment** — the conjunction of sun and moon. Whether an observer reckons the new moon as closing Sha'ban or opening Ramadan depends on local sighting conditions and method of reckoning. The letters named one face of this reality; the Imam named both.

The passage closes with: "The matter is in the hand of Allah." That phrase is not a retreat into vagueness — it is the acknowledgement that **no fixed calculation can stand above living guidance**. The heavens move; so does the Imam's word.

notes.quote: A statement has come from Mawlana, the author of the letters
etymology: رسائل (epistles): from the root ر-س-ل, meaning to send or dispatch. The verb أَرْسَلَ means to send a messenger, and رَسُول is the messenger himself. A single رِسَالَة is literally a "sending" — a mind dispatched across distance. The plural رَسَائِل names multiple such dispatches, each carrying the sender's thought to a distant reader.

إخوان (brethren): the singular is أَخ, from the root أ-خ-و, which expresses the closeness of those who cleave to one another. Naming the letter-writers إخوان places their community not among mere colleagues but among people bound by deep, chosen kinship — a brotherhood of souls, not simply of shared opinion.

صَفَاء (purity): from the root ص-ف-و, meaning to be clear, limpid, and free of sediment — as still water that settles into transparency. الصَّفَاء is that quality of settled clarity. The title إخوان الصفا names its members as brothers of clear-heartedness: people whose inner selves have been stilled and made transparent to the light.

تأويل (inner interpretation): from the root أ-و-ل, meaning to return a thing to its origin. أَوَّلَ is to trace back to a first principle. تأويل is the act of returning a word or event to its true, originary meaning — peeling back the surface to find what first gave it form. This is the Imam's living capacity, demonstrated precisely here.

دعوة (mission): from the root د-ع-و, meaning to call or summon. دَعَا is to call out, and الدَّاعِي is the one who calls. The دعوة is the Imam's living summons sent through trained emissaries into the world, carrying his knowledge and authority to all who hear and respond.

notes.body:
The passage raises a question it leaves deliberately unanswered. It cites "the books of the friends of Allah (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ)" without naming any of them, then closes with the phrase "so know this" — a classic Ismaili literary signal that the deeper truth must be sought through the living chain of guidance, not extracted from a page alone.

In Ismaili thought, **every outward act carries an inward reality** — the exoteric (ظاهر) and the esoteric (باطن) are always paired. The sunnah of dawn sits at a uniquely charged moment: Mawlana Ali himself said that after these two bowings, "the things most desired are granted." The permission to pray them before physical dawn has spread follows a spiritual logic — the soul's inner orientation toward divine light is not bound by any horizon.

The literature of interpretation (تَأْوِيل) produced by the Imams and their representatives is the body of work the text gestures toward without naming. Works like تَأْوِيلُ الدَّعَائِمِ — cited elsewhere in the same chapter — belong to this family of texts that unpack the hidden realities beneath outward worship. The path (سبيل) into those realities runs from the living Imam downward to those ready to receive it — and سبيل itself, at its root, names something let loose to hang freely and carry what it was sent to carry.

**Spiritual dawn precedes physical dawn.** The light of the Imam's guidance is not tied to any astronomical reckoning; when the soul has already turned toward that light, the outward condition of spreading dawn becomes secondary.
notes.anchor: it is permissible to pray it before dawn, on account of the noble mea…
notes.quote: it is permissible to pray it before dawn, on account of the noble meaning beneath this that permits it
etymology: سَبِيل (path): root س-ب-ل. Lane's Lexicon: سَبَل is something let loose to hang and flow freely toward the ground. A سَبِيل — road, channel, way — is what pours downward from its source to those who travel it. The title سَبِيلُ الْهُدَى captures this exactly: guidance is something that flows clearly down to the one seeking it.

فَجْر (dawn): root ف-ج-ر, to burst or split open with force. Dawn is the moment darkness is violently ruptured by light — not a gentle fading but a sudden breaking. The spiritual intensity of the sunnah of فَجْر belongs to this image: the night does not yield; it is split open.

بَاطِن (the inward): root ب-ط-ن, the belly or interior of something — what it holds within, unseen from outside. In Ismaili hermeneutics, every exoteric form (ظاهر) has a بَاطِن that is its living core, the purpose the outward act was made to carry.

مَعْنَى (meaning): root ع-ن-ي, to intend or to be occupied with something. The مَعْنَى of an act is what was always intended beneath its outer form — the inner aim the outward ruling exists to protect. The noble meaning (المعنى الشريف) is precisely that aimed-at truth concealed beneath the apparent ruling.

تَأْوِيل (interpretation): root أ-و-ل. تَأْوِيل is the act of returning something to its أَوَّل — its first and original meaning. Just as a traveler returns to the source, تَأْوِيل takes the outward text back to its deepest intent. In Ismaili thought, it is the living science entrusted to the Imam.

notes.body:
The passage presents a layered attribution. Mawlana Jafar first cites the historical Imam al-Sadiq (ع) as the source of the original ruling — that the prayer of Umm Daud was prescribed only for the month of Rajab, and that he commanded her to purify herself.

Then the register suddenly shifts: "And when I asked him about it, and whether that supplication may be recited in a month other than Rajab, he said..." A living, responsive voice answers with a new ruling about the day of ʿArafah and Fridays. **The grammar points unmistakably to a contemporary, not a historical figure.** Mawlana Jafar is writing from Yemen in or around the eleventh century of the Islamic era — centuries after the historical Imam al-Sadiq left this world.

The "him" must therefore be a living authority in Mawlana Jafar's own era. In the Tayyibi tradition, where the Imam al-Tayyib is in concealment (غيبة), the absolute representative (الداعي المطلق) holds delegated Imamic authority, and his words carry the standing of a binding text (نص). A second possibility that Ismaili spiritual literature allows: Mawlana Jafar, as a senior figure in the mission (دعوة), is describing a consultation that ran upward through the living chain of the hierarchy to the hidden Imam al-Tayyib himself — not met in the flesh, but reached through the vertical connection that binds every rank to the one above.

**Either way, the ruling does not stop with history.** It flows through a living pole in every age, and the "him" of this passage is that pole.
notes.anchor: when I asked him about it, and whether that supplication may be recit…
notes.quote: when I asked him about it, and whether that supplication may be recited in a month other than Rajab, he said
etymology: نص (authoritative text): from the root ن-ص-ص, meaning to raise something up so it stands visible and plain. A نص is a ruling 'stood upright' where everyone can see it — explicit, unambiguous, not buried in inference. This is why the passage insists a practice needs a نص before it is valid: it must stand up openly, not merely be assumed.

بدعة (innovation): from the root ب-د-ع, meaning to bring something into existence that had no prior model. The same root gives بديع, meaning wondrous or unprecedented. A بدعة in religious practice is an act 'originated' without grounding in the transmitted tradition — however sincere the intention, it lacks the standing of what was handed down.

دعوة (mission, call): from the root د-ع-و, meaning to call out, to summon, to invite. The root gives both دعوة (a summons, a mission) and داعي (the caller, the summoner). In Ismaili usage, the دعوة is the living mission that calls souls toward the Imam, and the داعي is the one who carries that call forward in every age.

notes.body:
*Researched outside this library — the knowledge base carries nothing on this passage. Sources are listed at the end.*

In the rich tapestry of Islamic practice, when reciting the Quran, there are certain verses that invite the reader or listener into a profound act of humility: the prostration of recitation (سجود التلاوة). This physical act of bowing down is a beautiful, immediate response to the divine word. However, not all of these verses carry the same weight of obligation; some are considered "binding" or obligatory, while others are highly recommended.

The distinction between a binding and a non-binding prostration is based on the teachings and practices of the Prophet Muhammad and the Imams who followed him. Within the broader Islamic tradition, there is a consensus on certain verses being obligatory, while the status of others varies among different schools of thought. For Ismailis, the authority flows from the Prophet and, through him, to the Imams.

The verses that are considered binding, often referred to as the prostrations of determination (عزائم السجود), are four specific passages in the Quran. When one recites or hears these particular verses, performing a prostration becomes an immediate obligation. These four verses are:
- As-Sajdah 32:15
- Fussilat 41:37-38
- An-Najm 53:62
- Al-Alaq 96:19

These are set apart because they contain a direct command to prostrate or describe the prostration of believers in such a powerful way that it compels an immediate physical response of submission.

Beyond these four, there are other verses in the Quran, numbering around eleven, where prostration is highly recommended but not strictly obligatory. Reciting these verses also calls for a prostration as an act of devotion and humility, following the Sunnah, or practice, of the Prophet. The principle behind this distinction is the emphasis placed on these specific four verses by the Prophet and the Imams, marking them as moments of essential and undeniable submission to Allah.

***

عزائم (determination): From the root ع-ز-م, which means to determine, to resolve, or to be set upon something. The word عزائم refers to things that are firmly decided or obligatory. In this context, it signifies that the prostration for these specific verses is a determined, binding command, not a matter of choice.
